## When the math works out exactly

On the previous page the posterior came from a numerical grid. For some
prior–likelihood pairs we don't need that, because the posterior has a closed form.

> A prior is **conjugate** to a likelihood if the posterior belongs to the
> **same family** as the prior. Updating then only changes the parameters.

## Beta-Binomial

Take a $\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ prior and $k$ heads in $n$ flips. Multiply
the prior and the likelihood, and drop every factor that doesn't depend on $\theta$:

$$
p(\theta \mid k) \;\propto\;
\underbrace{\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}}_{\text{likelihood}}\;
\underbrace{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}_{\text{prior}}
= \theta^{(\alpha + k) - 1}(1-\theta)^{(\beta + n - k) - 1}.
$$

That is again the kernel of a Beta density, so

$$
\boxed{\;\theta \mid k \;\sim\; \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\; \beta + n - k)\;}
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid k] = \frac{\alpha + k}{\alpha + \beta + n}.
$$

This is the pseudo-count reading from the Priors page made exact: **add the heads to
$\alpha$ and the tails to $\beta$**. The posterior mean sits between the prior
mean $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and the data proportion $k/n$, and it moves towards
$k/n$ as $n$ grows.

A useful consequence is that **sequential updating** gives the same result as one batch update.
Today's posterior is tomorrow's prior, and updating flip by flip ends in exactly the
same Beta as updating once with all the flips.

## Normal-Normal (known noise)

Second example: we measure a quantity $\mu$ with noise of known standard deviation
$\sigma$, so $x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, and we use the prior
$\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)$. The posterior is again Normal:

$$
\frac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \frac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2},
\qquad
\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left( \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{\sum_i x_i}{\sigma^2} \right).
$$

In words: the **precisions** (inverse variances) add up, and the posterior mean is a
precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data.

## Common conjugate pairs

| Likelihood | Parameter | Conjugate prior | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binomial / Bernoulli | success probability $\theta$ | Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$ | Beta$(\alpha + k, \beta + n - k)$ |
| Normal, known $\sigma$ | mean $\mu$ | Normal$(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)$ | Normal$(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)$ (above) |
| Poisson | rate $\lambda$ | Gamma$(a, b)$ | Gamma$(a + \sum x_i,\; b + n)$ |
| Categorical / Multinomial | probabilities $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ | Dirichlet$(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ | Dirichlet$(\boldsymbol{\alpha} + \text{counts})$ |

Conjugacy is fast and exact, but it only covers a narrow set of models. Most real
models have no conjugate prior, and the next two pages deal with that case.

## Interactive figure: updating flip by flip

A coin with true heads probability $\theta^\star$ is flipped 100 times (the sequence is fixed).
The slider "flips seen" reveals the flips one at a time. The solid line is the
conjugate posterior $\text{Beta}(\alpha + k, \beta + m - k)$ after $m$ flips. The dots
are the grid posterior from the previous page, computed independently. They lie on
the line: the two methods agree.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof theta_true = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {step: 0.05, value: 0.7, label: "true θ*"})
viewof m = Inputs.range([0, 100], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "flips seen"})
viewof alpha = Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "prior α"})
viewof beta = Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "prior β"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - theta_true
#|   - m
#|   - alpha
#|   - beta
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from bayes import beta_binomial_posterior, grid_posterior

# Fixed random stream, so moving "flips seen" reveals the same sequence.
u = np.random.default_rng(31).random(100)
flips = u < float(theta_true)
m_, a0, b0 = int(m), float(alpha), float(beta)
k_ = int(flips[:m_].sum())

a_post, b_post = beta_binomial_posterior(a0, b0, k_, m_)
theta = np.linspace(0.0005, 0.9995, 1000)
dtheta = theta[1] - theta[0]
grid = grid_posterior(theta, a0, b0, k_, m_) / dtheta  # independent numerical check

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.plot(theta, stats.beta.pdf(theta, a0, b0), "--", color="gray", label="prior")
ax.plot(theta, stats.beta.pdf(theta, a_post, b_post), lw=2, label=f"conjugate Beta({a_post:g}, {b_post:g})")
ax.plot(theta[::40], grid[::40], "o", ms=4, label="grid posterior")
ax.axvline(float(theta_true), color="C3", ls=":", label="true θ*")
seq = "".join("H" if f else "T" for f in flips[:m_])
ax.set_title(f"{k_} heads in {m_} flips   last: {seq[-20:] or '-'}", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("θ (probability of heads)")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise: update by hand

The prior is $\text{Beta}(2, 2)$. You flip the coin 10 times and observe

<p style="text-align:center; font-family:monospace; font-size:1.2em">H T H H T H H H T H</p>

Use the conjugate update to give the posterior parameters and the posterior mean
(as a number; 3 decimals is enough).

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_conj
alpha_post = ______
beta_post = ______
post_mean = ______
(alpha_post, beta_post, post_mean)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_conj
#| check: true
from bayes.checks import check_conjugate_update
ok, msg = check_conjugate_update(result, alpha=2, beta=2, k=7, n=10)
feedback = {"correct": ok, "message": msg}
feedback
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_conj" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false" }
Count the heads $k$ and the tails $n - k$. Then use
$\text{Beta}(\alpha + k, \beta + n - k)$ and the mean $\alpha' / (\alpha' + \beta')$.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_conj" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false" }
There are 7 heads and 3 tails, so the posterior is $\text{Beta}(9, 5)$ with mean $9/14 \approx 0.643$.

```python
alpha_post = 2 + 7
beta_post = 2 + 3
post_mean = alpha_post / (alpha_post + beta_post)
(alpha_post, beta_post, post_mean)
```
:::
:::
